kp.k: AI research competes through speed and complete platform functionality
kp.d: Von Zastrow describes MidPage as covering case law, statutes and regulations, with citator and case-history functionality needed to compete with established research platforms. He reports use by a couple hundred firms, from small firms to large firms, as either a replacement or a complement. His claim that some searches take minutes rather than an hour is a vendor assertion, not a reported comparative study; he stresses that superior search alone cannot displace established workflows.
qs: we can actually have a really different search experience that allows you to do some searches in just a couple of minutes that would have taken you maybe an hour before with
So even if it’s better at one thing, it doesn’t mean that you can replace your old ways of doing things until you have all those other items on the checklist too.
And this would, for example, be a good citator where you can see was this case overruled? What are all the other opinions that cite this case? What did the later court say about this?

kp.k: Grid-based research shifts case screening into structured comparison
kp.d: Von Zastrow says MidPage turns conventional search results into a spreadsheet-like comparison in which lawyers specify questions about outcomes, facts or clauses. AI classifies results against those questions, allowing lawyers to narrow hundreds or thousands of potentially relevant cases without individually opening and reading them all. He presents this as giving lawyers greater control, and identifies the interface as a pattern also appearing in transactional law and other industries.
qs: you can turn this whole classical search into a spreadsheet. every column can be a question that you care about.
And that, I feel, is a way to give more control back to the lawyers without them having to, you know, open up a hundred tabs and read every case.
It’s like having a Google search, but instead of just this one-dimensional list, you now have a multidimensional list.

kp.k: Proposition search combines judicial language with contextual filtering
kp.d: Responding to the host's comparison with CaseText's parallel search, von Zastrow attributes MidPage's proposition-search improvements to stronger models, a condensed interface and natural-language filters. He describes finding judicial statements supporting an argument while displaying procedural history and factual context alongside them, then filtering for particular factual conditions. These are product and comparative-quality claims without independent performance results in the transcript.
qs: Now three years later, the AI that is powering the search engine under the hood is just a lot stronger than it used to be.
And with our interface, you kind of get this very clean side-by-side view of here’s exactly the phrase that the judge said or wrote.
It’s a better search engine, it’s a great interface, and it’s sort of these powerful filtering options.

kp.k: Research repositories support continuity across complex investigations
kp.d: Von Zastrow identifies information overload and fear of missing important precedent as central research problems. He says organized search comparisons and the ability to chat with opinions collected in a shared research notebook help lawyers keep findings structured across several days of work. The emphasis is on supporting lawyer-led research rather than replacing legal judgment.
qs: most of the time during research is really just spent being overwhelmed by this huge mass of information and at the same time being really afraid of overlooking some very important precedent.

we also help try and sort of organize that by giving you some tools where you can chat with all the opinions that you’ve already found because they’re all part of your same notebook, your research repository.

kp.k: Legal expertise and simulated research inform product development
kp.d: Von Zastrow reports that a former Big Law litigator with a computer-science background became MidPage's strongest product manager. He also describes monthly legal-research exercises for employees, sometimes requiring traditional tools rather than MidPage, to expose engineers and designers to litigators' practical problems. This is an account of vendor product-development training, not evidence about law-firm associate formation.
qs: we hired a lawyer that used to work in Big Law as a litigator and he turned out to be our best product manager because he was the target user.
once a month we give them a legal research task where they have to use either classical tools or a mid-page to do research like they were a litigator.
then sometimes we forced them to do it the old way so that they know, you what are these features for?

kp.k: AI lowers historical legal-data barriers to market entry
kp.d: Von Zastrow argues that building extensive datasets and manually supplying citators, headnotes and procedural histories previously prevented startups from fully competing with Lexis and Westlaw, steering many toward contracts and transactional tools. He claims current AI can replace work previously requiring large annotation teams, making a full research platform feasible where it would have been impossible three years earlier. He nonetheless says construction remains laborious.
qs: legal research because you need to have this huge legal data set that is very hard to build.
they didn’t have,  an army of 2,000 people that are marking cases as overruled or not, like what the older players have, they just couldn’t afford that.
But at the time, they also didn’t have this really powerful AI that we have today that can replace that same job.
But now it’s doable. It’s still a lot of work.

kp.k: Expanded coverage could create new barriers and API markets
kp.d: Von Zastrow says incumbent manual approaches did not scale to what he describes as the 100 times larger volume of state trial-court cases. He plans broader coverage and predicts rising baseline expectations will eventually make entry harder again. He expects only a few suppliers to maintain high-quality datasets, but more than two; competition would, in his view, force API availability and enable other companies to build research-adjacent services. Separately, he predicts near-term consolidation among research vendors.
qs: It didn’t scale to the 100 times larger volume of cases coming from the state trial courts
when you add more and more things on top, it will actually start getting difficult again for new entrants.
obviously most of the work goes into ensuring the quality, not the completeness, but ensuring that everything is structured cleanly.
as soon as there’s competition, people will be forced to make this data available via APIs.
I think we’re now in this consolidation phase where probably the number of players is going to get smaller, not larger.

kp.k: Internal benchmarks and grounding underpin claimed hallucination controls
kp.d: Von Zastrow reports feature-specific evaluation pipelines using a handcrafted set of a couple hundred examples and around 10 AI features, selecting models according to internal benchmarks that include hallucination. He says outputs are grounded in original opinions with quotations and links for human verification, and claims hallucination is now nearly impossible in MidPage's systems. The transcript supplies no numerical scores or independent validation. His subsequent characterization of residual problems as vague or evasive answers distinguishes those from fabricated answers, rather than establishing a measured fabrication rate.
qs: for every feature that we have, we have an evaluation pipeline.
handcrafted set of a couple hundred examples, and maybe like around 10 different features that use AI.
And that score includes things like hallucination.
So it always bases it on the original opinion. And then it always quotes from that opinion and gives you a link so that you can open the opinion of that section.
And so both you can verify, and also it’s near to impossible to get our systems to hallucinate now, even if you try really hard on purpose.

kp.k: General chat requires access to relevant legal source material
kp.d: Von Zastrow attributes ChatGPT's fabricated legal answers to answering from memory without access to a case-law database. He describes a MidPage database plugin, while saying it is less powerful than MidPage's own interface. His immediate recommendation is to use ChatGPT only for questions whose necessary materials have been uploaded into the conversation; his expectation that database-access problems will soon be fixed is a prediction. The host, rather than the guest, introduces continuing court filings with invented citations.
qs: And ChatGPT does not have access to a caselaw database So then it tries to answer those things from memory without having any place to check or to look it up.
We actually even have a plugin where you can connect our database to ChatGPT.
for now I would just recommend everybody to only use ChatGPT for questions where all the material needed to answer those questions is uploaded directly in that chat.

kp.k: AI may intensify litigation research rather than reduce competition
kp.d: In his forward-looking answer, von Zastrow predicts deeper work product from the same litigator. His illustrative comparison moves from reading and assessing 100 cases in a week to processing 1,000 or 10,000 at the same depth next year or the year after, rather than reporting measured productivity. He expects both sides to become more capable, maintaining competitive pressure, and suggests small teams could handle previously inaccessible case types. His principal forecast is more exhaustive research, not specified staffing reductions or billing changes.
qs: These tools are like a multiplier on your existing talents, I would say.

So if maybe in the past a litigator was able to, in a week, maybe read and assess 100 cases, which would be a lot, next year or the year after, you’ll be able to process 1,000 cases or 10,000 cases with the same level of… of depth
think small teams can handle maybe new types of cases that they wouldn’t be able to handle before.
So I feel that’s where we’re headed more depth.

kp.k: Client self-education may improve understanding while introducing mistakes
kp.d: Von Zastrow predicts clients will use ChatGPT to educate themselves about legal matters, analogizing to patients' use of it for medical questions. Particularly in small-firm settings where clients press for minimal research, he expects greater understanding of lawyers' work and possible self-resolution of easier questions, alongside mistaken ideas about what lawyers should do. He presents these as prospective possibilities rather than demonstrated improvements in access to justice.
qs: They will use ChatGPT like they’re using it for their doctor as well. they will come up with some wrong things that they think you ought to do as a lawyer.
that they have a way of understanding your work much better than before.
And maybe that they can even solve some of easier questions themselves, even though you as a lawyer might be afraid of letting them do that.

kp.k: Agentic retrieval may matter more than image understanding
kp.d: Von Zastrow expects image understanding alone to have limited impact on legal research. He instead emphasizes models navigating websites, retrieving newly filed regulations or guidance, and comparing them with research-platform versions to detect outdated material. He describes some such capabilities as already occurring and predicts longer sequences of actions on users' behalf, making multimodality important for interaction with external systems rather than simply adding images to research.
qs: at least for legal research, being able to understand images is not going to have a huge effect.
These models can now by themselves do some Google searches, go out to the internet, they can click around a certain website
they can compare that to the version that is in your research platform and notice that it’s maybe not quite up to date anymore.
The models will also just take way longer sequences of actions in the real world on your behalf, whether you’re doing research or something else.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Otto von Zastrow claims AI makes legal research faster, more precise and easier to organise; lowers barriers to building research platforms; and will increase lawyers’ research depth and clients’ ability to inform themselves.
pts.d: Von Zastrow describes MidPage’s grid-based search, proposition search, natural-language filters and research notebooks as ways to narrow large result sets, compare facts and procedural histories, locate supporting judicial language and organise findings. He claims some searches take minutes rather than approximately an hour. He argues that contemporary AI can perform legal-data enrichment work previously requiring large human teams, making competing research platforms feasible. He predicts near-term consolidation alongside greater competition than the historical two-provider landscape, more abundant legal data and competitive pressure to provide APIs for downstream research and drafting tools. He claims grounded, purpose-designed systems such as MidPage now make fabricated output extremely difficult to elicit. His longer-term forecast principally concerns augmentation: lawyers will produce deeper work, small teams may handle new kinds of cases, and both sides of litigation will become more capable. Clients may answer simpler questions themselves but also bring mistaken AI-derived suggestions to lawyers. He expects models to execute longer sequences of online research and retrieval actions, rather than image understanding alone substantially transforming legal research.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is primarily von Zastrow’s product-building experience, reported adoption, feature descriptions and internal benchmarking; the market and productivity forecasts are not accompanied by published quantitative results.
pts.d: At 06:45, von Zastrow reports current use by a couple hundred firms, including users replacing incumbent platforms and others supplementing them. At 11:14, he describes product development led by a former Big Law litigator with a computer-science background and monthly research exercises for employees. For reliability, at 24:14 he describes feature-specific evaluation pipelines, handcrafted sets of a couple hundred examples, roughly ten AI features, model selection using internal benchmarks and scores that include hallucination. He also describes grounding in original opinions, quotations and links that enable human verification. No numerical hallucination scores, comparative research-speed measurements or independent validation are supplied in the interview. His market forecasts draw on his account of historical dataset and staffing barriers and current technical capabilities. His forecast of processing thousands of cases at comparable depth is illustrative, not presented as a measured result. As a cross-domain motivation, he estimates a 20% programmer productivity boost from GitHub Copilot without citing a study.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Von Zastrow distinguishes capabilities he describes as current from forecasts over the next one to several years, and qualifies adoption and reliability by platform completeness, data quality and access to source material.
pts.d: Speaking in the supplied 2025 interview, he says independent datasets should become more accessible over the next couple of years and that building a competitive research platform is now feasible where it would have been impossible three years earlier. Replacement of incumbents requires the full set of expected functions, including a citator and case history, not merely one superior feature. He expects expansion into state trial-court data to raise the competitive baseline and eventually make entry harder again; maintaining structured, high-quality data remains substantial work. His strongest reliability claims concern narrowly designed, source-grounded features, while he acknowledges fabrication when models are asked questions they cannot know. He expects ChatGPT’s legal-data access problem to be fixed soon, but meanwhile recommends supplying all necessary material directly in the chat. In the next year or two, he forecasts lawyers processing 1,000 or 10,000 cases rather than an illustrative 100 in a week at comparable depth. He describes models’ online interaction capabilities as already emerging, while predicting longer action sequences. He does not assign precise dates to API availability, consolidation or client self-service.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are litigators and other researchers, firms of different sizes, legal-data and software providers, and clients seeking cheaper answers or greater understanding of legal work.
pts.d: Von Zastrow identifies litigators as the main users, alongside other lawyers, and reports adoption ranging from small firms to Big Law. Lawyers gain control over large result sets and greater research capacity; small teams may become able to undertake matters previously beyond them, while major litigation becomes more exhaustive without necessarily reducing competitive pressure because opposing teams have similar tools. Small-firm clients seeking efficiency may become better informed and answer simple questions themselves, but may also misunderstand AI-generated information. Incumbent legal-research providers face new competition and potential pressure to open data through APIs; specialist software developers could build services on those datasets. He nevertheless expects only a few organisations to maintain comprehensive, high-quality legal data. His claim that AI can replace human case-marking work concerns legal-data production; he does not provide a forecast of law-firm staffing reductions or measured employment effects.
